data.universal_indicator_turns_a_different_co: Universal Indicator turns a different colour for every strength of acid and alkali, making a rainbow from red to purple. Red means a strong acid, orange and yellow mean weaker acids, and green means neutral. Green is pH 7, the pH of pure water, which is also why the indicator liquid itself looks green in the bottle. Blue and purple mean alkalis, and the deeper the purple, the stronger the alkali. In your results, lemon juice was red, vinegar orange, water green, bicarbonate blue-green and bleach purple, so the colours placed each liquid on the pH scale.
data.litmus_paper_only_gives_you_two_possible: Litmus paper only gives you two possible answers: it turns red in an acid and blue in an alkali. In neutral water it stays purple. It cannot tell you how strong the acid or alkali is, because lemon juice and vinegar both turned it the same red. That is why litmus is a quick first test, while Universal Indicator is better when you need detail. Scientists often use litmus to decide which side of the pH scale a solution is on before they test it more carefully.
data.phenolphthalein_is_completely_colourless: Phenolphthalein is completely colourless in acids and in neutral solutions, so it looks as if nothing has happened. It only reacts to alkalis, turning pink. The stronger the alkali, the brighter the pink, so bicarbonate gave a faint pink and bleach gave a bright pink. Because the change is so sudden, chemists use it in titrations to spot the exact moment an acid has been used up. This makes it a very precise tool for alkalis, but it tells you nothing about acids.
data.lemon_juice_and_vinegar_are_acids_water_: Lemon juice and vinegar are acids, water is neutral, and bicarbonate and bleach are alkalis. All three indicators agreed with each other, which makes the conclusion more reliable. Litmus sorted the liquids into acid, neutral and alkali, phenolphthalein picked out only the alkalis, and Universal Indicator gave each liquid its own place on the pH scale. Each indicator is a different tool, and each tells you something the others cannot. Scientists combine evidence from more than one test, just as you did, before they trust a result.

Then pull slowly and steadily along the ramp. Look straight at the scale and read the number the pointer is level with. The unit is newtons, written N.
data.gravity_pulls_every_object_down_that_pul: Gravity pulls every object down. That pull is its weight, W. We work it out with W = m × g. W is the weight in newtons (N), m is the mass in kilograms (kg), and g is the pull of gravity, about 10 N for every 1 kg. Our block has a mass of 0.5 kg, so W = 0.5 × 10 = 5 N.
data.on_a_flat_ramp_the_ramp_holds_up_all_of_: On a flat ramp, the ramp holds up all of the block's weight, so you only pull against a little friction. Tilt the ramp and it holds up less of the weight. Your pull has to do more of the work to stop the block sliding back down. The steeper the ramp, the more of the 5 N weight you have to pull against, so the Newton meter reading goes up.
data.the_steeper_the_ramp_the_bigger_the_forc: The steeper the ramp, the bigger the force on the Newton meter. At 0° it was only about 0.3 N, and at 60° it was about 4.3 N. If the ramp were straight up, you would pull with the whole weight, W = mg = 5 N. Your line of best fit shows it: as the angle goes up, the force goes up.

The tripod stands over the burner and holds the wire gauze, which spreads the heat out evenly. The dish of solution sits on the gauze. Always check that the tube is on tight and the collar is closed before you light the match.
data.the_collar_on_the_burner_lets_air_into_t: The collar on the burner lets air into the barrel, and air contains oxygen. With the collar closed, no extra oxygen gets in, so you get the yellow safety flame. It is cooler, easy to see, and used for lighting. With the collar open, the most oxygen gets in and you get the blue roaring flame. It is much hotter and leaves no soot, so it is the one we use for heating.
data.to_observe_a_change_look_carefully_and_w: To observe a change, look carefully and write down what you see. Check the colour, whether it is a solid, a liquid or a gas, and whether anything is given off, like steam. In the dish, the water left as steam and the blue solution became a white powder solid. Changes like this, where the substance can be got back again, are physical changes. Ice melting and water boiling are physical changes too.
data.physical_changes_can_be_reversed_melted_: Physical changes can be reversed. Melted ice can be frozen again, and when we added water to the white powder it turned blue again. Chemical changes cannot be reversed. When wood burns it turns into ash, smoke and gases, and you can never turn it back into wood. So if you can get the original substance back, it is a physical change. If you cannot, it is a chemical change.

data.the_coverslip_flattens_the_sample_and_pr: The coverslip flattens the sample and protects the lens. Lower it slowly at an angle, so air bubbles do not get trapped, because bubbles can look like cells and spoil the view.
data.slide_prepared_time_to_load_it_onto_the_: Slide prepared! Time to load it onto the microscope.
data.angle_the_coverslip_into_the_green_zone_: Angle the coverslip into the green zone before lowering.
data.drag_the_microscope_onto_the_bench_cug7: Drag the microscope onto the bench.
data.the_microscope_makes_tiny_things_look_mu: The microscope makes tiny things look much bigger, so we can see cells that are far too small for our eyes. Put it on a flat, steady bench, and always carry it with two hands.
data.microscope_set_up_now_load_your_slide_on: Microscope set up. Now load your slide onto the stage.
data.drag_your_prepared_slide_onto_the_micros: Drag your prepared slide onto the microscope stage.
data.the_slide_goes_flat_on_the_stage_under_t: The slide goes flat on the stage, under the clips, so it cannot slip. Light shines up from below through your sample, and the lenses above magnify it.
data.slide_loaded_and_clipped_in_place_now_se: Slide loaded and clipped in place. Now set the lens and the light.
data.drag_the_slide_onto_the_stage_10hk: Drag the slide onto the stage.
data.spin_the_microscope_and_tap_each_part_to: Spin the microscope and tap each part to find out what it does.
data.a_microscope_makes_tiny_things_look_much: A microscope makes tiny things look much bigger, so we can see cells that are far too small for our eyes. Drag to spin it, scroll or pinch to zoom, and tap any part to learn about it.
data.light_shines_up_from_the_lamp_through_yo: Light shines up from the lamp, through your slide on the stage, and into the lenses. The lenses bend the light to make the picture bigger.
data.to_find_the_total_magnification_multiply: To find the total magnification, multiply the eyepiece by the objective lens. The eyepiece is ×10, so the ×4 lens gives ×40, the ×10 lens gives ×100 and the ×40 lens gives ×400.
data.when_you_have_explored_every_part_press_: When you have explored every part, press Complete and we will use the microscope for real.
data.now_you_know_every_part_time_to_use_the_: Now you know every part! Time to use the microscope for real.
data.tap_the_parts_to_explore_them_then_press: Tap the parts to explore them, then press Complete.
data.turn_on_the_light_select_each_lens_in_tu: Turn on the light, select each lens in turn, focus, and centre a cell.
data.start_with_the_lowest_power_lens_to_find: Start with the lowest-power lens to find the cells, then move to a stronger lens and use the focus to make the picture sharp. Never wind the lens down while looking through the eyepiece, because it could hit the slide.
data.there_they_are_pip_s_cheek_cells_stained: There they are! Pip's cheek cells, stained blue so we can see the structures.
data.work_through_each_control_in_order_light: Work through each control in order: light, lens, focus, stage.
data.turn_each_page_to_label_the_parts_of_you: Turn each page to label the parts of your cheek cell.
data.the_cell_membrane_is_the_thin_skin_aroun: The cell membrane is the thin skin around the cell. It is soft and bendy, so the edge of a cheek cell looks rounded and a bit wobbly. It also decides what can go in and out of the cell.
data.the_nucleus_is_the_dark_blue_dot_in_the_: The nucleus is the dark blue dot in the middle. It is the control centre of the cell. It holds the instructions that tell the cell how to work and how to make new cells.
data.the_cytoplasm_is_the_pale_blue_jelly_tha: The cytoplasm is the pale blue jelly that fills the cell. Most of the cell's jobs happen here. The stain made it blue so you could see it.
data.look_at_the_edge_of_your_cell_there_is_n: Look at the edge of your cell. There is no hard cell wall, only the soft membrane. Plant cells do have a cell wall. That is how we know these are animal cells.
data.tap_every_part_of_the_cell_fxgw: Tap every part of the cell.
data.rapid_fire_answer_before_the_timer_runs_: Rapid-fire! Answer before the timer runs out.
data.what_controls_what_enters_the_cell_g7bm: What controls what enters the cell?
data.what_would_not_be_found_in_pip_s_cheek_c: What would NOT be found in Pip's cheek cells?
data.it_stains_the_nucleus_to_make_it_visible: It stains the nucleus to make it visible
data.read_each_slide_to_understand_what_you_d: Read each slide to understand what you did and saw.
data.cheek_cells_are_a_safe_easy_way_to_see_a: Cheek cells are a safe, easy way to see animal cells. Rub a clean cotton swab gently on the inside of your cheek. Always use your own fresh swab and never share one, because germs can pass between people. Once you have smeared the sample on the slide, put the swab straight into disinfectant and wash your hands. Hold glass slides by the edges so they do not cut you.
data.put_the_microscope_on_a_flat_bench_and_s: Put the microscope on a flat bench and switch on the light. Start with the lowest-power lens and use the focus knob to make the picture sharp. Then move to a stronger lens to see more detail, and focus again. Always carry the microscope with two hands, and let the light cool down before you pack it away.
data.a_microscope_lets_you_see_the_shape_and_: A microscope lets you see the shape and the parts of a cell. In stained cheek cells you can see a dark blue nucleus in the middle, paler blue cytoplasm around it, and a thin cell membrane at the edge. The stain is needed because cheek cells are almost see-through. Some parts, like mitochondria, are too tiny to see with a school microscope.
data.let_s_compare_animal_cells_and_plant_cel: Let's compare! Animal cells and plant cells both have a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane. Only plant cells also have a cell wall, a big vacuole and chloroplasts. The cell wall gives plant cells a neat, fixed shape, while animal cells, like your cheek cells, look rounder and less regular. Chloroplasts let plants make food using light, and animal cells never have them.
data.you_understood_the_biology_that_s_the_wh: You understood the biology. That's the whole point.
data.never_handle_a_circuit_with_wet_hands_5n: Never handle a circuit with wet hands.
data.check_and_before_connecting_the_wrong_wa: Check + and − before connecting, the wrong way round can damage the battery.
data.disconnect_a_wire_before_rearranging_any: Disconnect a wire before rearranging any part of the circuit.
data.safety_checks_done_let_s_build_your_firs: Safety checks done. Let's build your first circuit.
data.drag_each_part_onto_its_dashed_spot_then: Drag each part onto its dashed spot, then drag a wire from one connector to the next.
data.the_bulb_is_on_the_circuit_is_complete_g: THE BULB IS ON! The circuit is complete, electrons are flowing!
data.wire_every_connector_then_close_the_swit: Wire every connector, then close the switch.
data.place_the_ammeter_in_series_wire_it_in_t: Place the ammeter in series, wire it in, then close the switch and read it.
data.0_3_amperes_same_current_everywhere_in_a: 0.3 amperes. Same current everywhere in a series circuit.
data.0_3a_that_current_is_the_same_everywhere: 0.3A, that current is the same everywhere in this loop.
data.an_ammeter_must_sit_in_series_in_the_loo: An ammeter must sit in series, in the loop itself.
data.place_the_voltmeter_across_the_bulb_both: Place the voltmeter ACROSS the bulb, both its terminals connect to the bulb, not the main loop.
data.v_ir_1_5_0_3_5_ohms_that_s_the_bulb_s_re: V = IR. 1.5 ÷ 0.3 = 5 ohms. That’s the bulb’s resistance.
data.1_5v_across_the_bulb_a_voltmeter_always_: 1.5V across the bulb, a voltmeter always connects in parallel.
data.the_voltmeter_needs_both_terminals_on_th: The voltmeter needs both terminals on the bulb, not the main loop.
data.replicate_the_diagram_a_bulb_in_parallel: Replicate the diagram, a bulb in PARALLEL with a motor.
data.the_motor_connects_across_the_bulb_not_i: The motor connects across the bulb, not in series.
data.read_each_slide_to_understand_your_circu: Read each slide to understand your circuits.
data.an_electric_circuit_is_a_loop_that_elect: An electric circuit is a loop that electricity can travel all the way around. The battery pushes the electricity, the wires carry it, and the bulb uses it to make light. If there is a gap anywhere in the loop, the electricity stops. That is why a torch only works when everything inside it is joined up in one complete loop.
data.a_switch_is_a_gap_in_the_circuit_that_yo: A switch is a gap in the circuit that you can open or close. When it is closed, the loop is complete and the bulb lights up. When it is open, there is a gap and everything switches off. You use switches all day: the light switch on the wall, the button on a torch and the power button on a game controller.
data.in_a_series_circuit_everything_is_on_one: In a series circuit, everything is on one single loop, like children holding hands in a ring. The same current goes through every part. If one part breaks, the whole loop stops. Old strings of fairy lights are wired like this, so one broken bulb can switch off the whole string. Add more bulbs to the loop and each one gets dimmer.
data.in_a_parallel_circuit_the_electricity_ha: In a parallel circuit, the electricity has more than one path to follow, like a road that splits in two. Each bulb has its own path, so if one bulb breaks, the others stay on. The lights in your home are wired in parallel. That is why you can switch off the kitchen light and the living room light stays on.
data.an_ammeter_measures_current_which_is_how: An ammeter measures current, which is how much electricity flows past each second. It goes in series, inside the loop. A voltmeter measures voltage, which is how hard the battery pushes. It goes in parallel, across the part you want to check. A phone charger is a real example, because it has its volts and amps printed on it.
data.circuits_are_everywhere_a_torch_a_bicycl: Circuits are everywhere. A torch, a bicycle light, a doorbell, a toy car and your phone all use circuits. The electricity from a wall socket is much stronger than a battery, so never poke anything into a socket and never touch a plug with wet hands. Fuses and circuit breakers switch a circuit off if too much electricity flows, to keep us safe.

mission.block1:
LabBudi is a virtual app platform that attempts to turn practical science into something students can explore.
This web app is a videogame-inspired, interactive virtual laboratory hosting a collection of these simulations, initially centred around iGCSE practicals for students aged 11 to 14.
Students can handle virtual equipment, change variables, make observations and work with real scientific datasets, while receiving feedback as they experiment.
The platform is being developed in multiple languages to reduce the language barrier, and its interface draws from the things that first made learning feel exciting to me: children's books, engaging illustrations and interactive games.
mission.block2: The goal is for each practical to feel like entering a little world of its own. A student might follow an illustrated trail into a virtual laboratory, uncover an experiment through a <green>storybook-like</green> interface, interact with equipment through play and discover the scientific reasoning behind their results. The goal is not to turn science into a game for the sake of being entertaining; it is to use interaction to make understanding active. I believe that students should be able to try something, <coral>get it wrong</coral>, <amber>wonder why</amber>, and <green>try again</green>.
mission.block3_s1: I first began thinking about barriers to understanding when I started my own science club.
mission.block3_s2: As I mentored younger students and watched the international student population grow, I began noticing how <coral>language</coral> could become a <coral>barrier</coral> to science itself.
mission.block3_s3: A student could be curious, capable and excited to learn, yet still struggle to understand a practical simply because the instructions were not in a language they were fully comfortable with.
mission.block3_s4: Sometimes, the hardest part of learning science is not the science itself, but being given a way to access it.
mission.block4: Volunteering with under-resourced communities showed me another side of that same problem. Here, the barrier was practical. Some students did not have consistent access to the laboratory equipment and experiments that I had come to take for granted at school. They could learn what a <blue>microscope</blue> was from a textbook, but not necessarily have the opportunity to use one. They could memorise the steps of an experiment without being able to explore what would happen if they changed something. I began to understand that <green>practical science</green> is not just about demonstrating knowledge; it is often how that <amber>knowledge becomes real</amber>.
mission.block5_body: And to the <amber>curious mind</amber> reading this now, I hope you are encouraged to continue this journey!
mission.block6: Much like the art seeded through the platform, the embodiment of LabBudi's vision of science is a vibrant, lively <green>garden</green>. Every student starts with different <amber>soil</amber>, different resources and different conditions. Some have laboratories filled with equipment; others do not. But curiosity is a <amber>seed</amber>, and understanding is what allows it to <green>grow</green>. LabBudi is a space to nurture and to give more students the space to plant that seed, explore what grows, and discover that they were <coral>never incapable</coral> of understanding science; they simply needed the opportunity to see it for themselves.
mission.quote: The flower that blooms in adversity is the most rare and beautiful of all.

scrap.note_lemon: Lemon juice is a strong food acid, pH 2. You squeeze it over fish and pancakes and into lemonade, and the sour taste you get is the acid.
scrap.note_vinegar: Vinegar is a weak acid, pH 4. It gives chips and salad dressing their tang, cooks use it to pickle vegetables, and at home it dissolves limescale in kettles.
scrap.note_water: Pure water is neutral, pH 7. It is in every tap, bottle and puddle, and it is the reference point that every other pH is measured against.
scrap.note_bicarb: Bicarbonate of soda is a weak alkali, pH 8. It makes cakes rise in the oven, and many people use it to soften bad smells in the fridge or to settle an upset stomach.
scrap.note_bleach: Bleach is a strong alkali, pH 13. It disinfects toilets and kitchen floors, but it burns skin, so always wear gloves and never mix it with other cleaning products.
